Async behavior::Async UI.summary: Wait for asynchronous UI transitions with findBy and waitFor. Use findBy for an eventual element and waitFor for assertions that must be retried until they pass.
Async behavior::Async UI.explanation: Async UI tests await state transitions instead of asserting immediately. Use a findBy query when one matching element should eventually appear; use waitFor when an assertion must be retried until it stops throwing.
Async behavior::Async UI.syntax: function waitFor<T>(callback: () => T | Promise<T>, options?: { container?: HTMLElement; timeout?: number; interval?: number; onTimeout?: (error: Error) => Error; mutationObserverOptions?: MutationObserverInit }): Promise<T>

parameters.name: callback
parameters.description: A callback returning a value or promise that waitFor retries until it succeeds.

parameters.name: options
parameters.type: { container?: HTMLElement; timeout?: number; interval?: number; onTimeout?: (error: Error) => Error; mutationObserverOptions?: MutationObserverInit }
parameters.description: Optional container, timeout, interval, timeout handler, and mutation-observer settings.

Async behavior::Async UI.returns: waitFor returns a Promise<T>; findBy queries return promises that resolve when the query succeeds.

example.title: Await loading and success states
example.explanation: The test checks the immediate loading state, then awaits the eventual success state and a related DOM assertion.

useCases.title: Await an eventual result
useCases.scenario: A loading indicator is replaced by a result after a request resolves.

useCases.title: Retry an assertion
useCases.scenario: A state change requires checking several DOM conditions.

useCases.title: Verify disappearance
useCases.scenario: A dialog, spinner, or notification is removed after an interaction.

interview.question: When should you use findBy?
interview.answer: findBy combines a getBy query with waitFor and returns a promise. It is appropriate when the expected element should appear after an asynchronous DOM change.
interview.followUp: When should findAllBy be used? Use it when multiple matching elements are expected; findBy is for a single match and rejects when the result is ambiguous.

interview.question: How does waitFor retry assertions?
interview.answer: waitFor repeatedly invokes a callback until it no longer throws or its timeout is reached. Put the assertion inside the callback so the failed expectation triggers another attempt.
interview.followUp: What happens if the callback returns a pending promise? Retries pause until that promise rejects, which can delay or prevent the expected retry cycle.

interview.question: Why must async queries be awaited?
interview.answer: Async helpers return promises, so the test must await them or use .then. Without that synchronization, the test may proceed or complete before the asynchronous UI update is observed.
interview.followUp: How would you test removal instead of appearance? Use waitForElementToBeRemoved with a callback that queries the element during DOM mutations.

keyPoints: Use findBy when an element is expected to appear eventually: it combines single-element querying with asynchronous waiting.
A findBy call can receive query options first and waitFor options last, allowing its timeout and related waiting behavior to be customized.
Choose waitFor when the condition is an assertion or other callback result rather than simply finding one eventual element.
The waitFor callback can execute repeatedly, so its body should be safe to retry and should not perform non-idempotent actions.
Use waitForElementToBeRemoved for disappearance, rather than forcing an appearance-oriented query to represent removal.
gotchas: Always await findBy, waitFor, and other async helpers; otherwise the test can finish before the UI transition is verified.
An async waitFor callback pauses retries until its returned promise rejects, so avoid returning a promise unless that behavior is intentional.
For disappearance checks, queryBy is suitable because it returns null when absent; getBy throws before the outer assertion can inspect the result.

Async behavior::findBy and waitFor.summary: Use findBy to await one element that should appear asynchronously; use waitFor to retry an assertion or custom condition until it succeeds or times out. Await both because async Testing Library methods return Promises.
Async behavior::findBy and waitFor.explanation: Use a findBy query when a particular element should eventually appear; it combines an ordinary getBy query with waitFor and returns a Promise. Use waitFor when the condition is an assertion or requires custom logic: its callback is retried until it completes without throwing or the timeout is reached. Await either utility.
Async behavior::findBy and waitFor.syntax:
await screen.findByText(text, queryOptions?, waitForOptions?)
await waitFor(callback, options?)

parameters.name: callback
parameters.description: The waitFor callback, which returns a value or Promise and is retried until successful or timed out.

parameters.name: container
parameters.description: Optional container used for observing DOM mutations.

parameters.name: timeout
parameters.description: Optional maximum wait duration.

parameters.name: interval
parameters.description: Optional delay between callback attempts.

parameters.name: onTimeout
parameters.description: Optional function that transforms the timeout error.

parameters.name: mutationObserverOptions
parameters.description: Optional MutationObserver configuration.

Async behavior::findBy and waitFor.returns: findBy returns a Promise resolving to the matching element; waitFor resolves with the callback's result when the callback completes without throwing. Both reject or time out when the condition is not met.

example.title: Wait for an asynchronous message
example.code:
import {render, screen, fireEvent} from '@testing-library/react'
import '@testing-library/jest-dom'
import {App} from './App'

test('shows the saved message', async () => {
  render(<App />)
  fireEvent.click(screen.getByRole('button', {name: 'Save'}))

  expect(await screen.findByText('Saved')).toBeInTheDocument()
})
example.explanation: The test awaits a findBy query so it resolves after the asynchronous UI update produces the expected text.

useCases.title: Wait for appearance with findBy
useCases.scenario: A user action triggers rendering of one new element after asynchronous work.

useCases.title: Retry an assertion with waitFor
useCases.scenario: An update changes text, attributes, or another condition that needs an assertion.

useCases.title: Wait for custom logic
useCases.scenario: A callback must perform custom asynchronous verification rather than a single query.

interview.question: What is a findBy query, and when would you use it?
interview.answer: findBy queries are asynchronous combinations of getBy queries and waitFor. They return a Promise that resolves when the matching element is found, or rejects when the query cannot produce the expected result within the timeout.
interview.followUp: How do you pass timing configuration? Supply the query options first and the waitFor options as the final argument, such as findByText(text, queryOptions, waitForOptions).

interview.question: How does waitFor retry?
interview.answer: waitFor repeatedly invokes its callback until the callback stops throwing or the timeout is reached. It is useful when the condition is an assertion or cannot be expressed as one element query.
interview.followUp: What happens with an async callback? waitFor waits for its returned promise; it does not invoke the callback again until that promise rejects.

interview.question: How do you choose between findBy and waitFor?
interview.answer: Both utilities are asynchronous and must be awaited or handled with then. findBy is usually the direct choice for waiting for an element to appear, while waitFor wraps a broader expectation or custom condition.
interview.followUp: How would you test disappearance? Use waitForElementToBeRemoved, which waits for the queried element to leave the DOM.

keyPoints: findBy combines immediate single-match querying with asynchronous retrying, making it the concise choice for an element that will appear later.
A findBy call can receive normal query options followed by waitFor configuration, allowing matching and timing concerns to remain separate.
Use findBy when the DOM update is delayed after an interaction and the test expects one matching element to appear.
Use waitFor to retry an expectation rather than inserting a fixed sleep into the test.
waitFor retries the callback and finishes when it succeeds or when its configured timeout expires.
An asynchronous waitFor callback pauses further retries while its returned promise is pending.
gotchas: Async queries and wait utilities return Promises; omitting await can let the test finish before the asynchronous condition is checked.
A promise-returning waitFor callback is not retried until that promise rejects, so ensure the callback represents the intended retry condition.
The callback can execute repeatedly, so it should be safe to run more than once and should not perform one-time side effects.

Async behavior::MSW and network boundari.summary: Use MSW to declaratively mock API communication at the network boundary instead of stubbing fetch. This keeps component request logic realistic while tests assert loading, success, and error UI through the DOM.
Async behavior::MSW and network boundari.explanation: MSW intercepts HTTP communication outside the component, allowing the test to keep the real request path while controlling the server response. React Testing Library then verifies the loading, success, or failure UI through DOM queries and user interactions.

parameters.name: handlers
parameters.description: MSW request handlers define how matching API calls should respond.

parameters.name: component
parameters.description: The rendered React component under test initiates the request.

Async behavior::MSW and network boundari.returns: A controlled HTTP response that the component processes through its normal loading, success, or error path.

example.title: Test a successful request at the network boundary
example.code:
import {http, HttpResponse} from 'msw'
import {setupServer} from 'msw/node'
import {render, screen} from '@testing-library/react'
import userEvent from '@testing-library/user-event'
import Fetch from './Fetch'

const server = setupServer(
  http.get('/api/message', () =>
    HttpResponse.json({message: 'Hello'}),
  ),
)

beforeAll(() => server.listen())
afterEach(() => server.resetHandlers())
afterAll(() => server.close())

test('shows the fetched message', async () => {
  render(<Fetch />)
  await userEvent.click(screen.getByRole('button', {name: /load/i}))
  expect(await screen.findByText('Hello')).toBeInTheDocument()
})
example.explanation: MSW intercepts the component's request while the test observes the resulting UI.

useCases.title: Success states
useCases.scenario: Return successful data from an intercepted request and assert the rendered result.

useCases.title: Error states
useCases.scenario: Replace a handler with an error response and verify the user-visible failure state.

useCases.title: Loading behavior
useCases.scenario: Exercise asynchronous loading transitions without mocking component internals.

interview.question: Why use MSW instead of mocking fetch directly?
interview.answer: MSW is recommended because it mocks API communication declaratively at the request boundary instead of replacing `window.fetch`. The component follows its normal request code, so the test can assert the user-visible result.
interview.followUp: How would you cover a server failure? Override the matching request handler for that test so it returns an error response, then await and assert the rendered error state.

interview.question: How is an MSW server configured in a React Testing Library test?
interview.answer: Create handlers with MSW's HTTP API, pass them to `setupServer`, and start that server for the test environment. The supplied example uses `setupServer` to mock the API request made by the tested component.
interview.followUp: How do you keep per-test behavior isolated? Reset handlers after each test, then close the server after the suite so overrides do not leak.

interview.question: How do MSW and React Testing Library work together for async UI behavior?
interview.answer: The test should render the component, interact with it as a user would, and wait for the resulting DOM state. This exercises the asynchronous request flow without coupling the assertion to implementation details.
interview.followUp: What should a loading-state test assert? Trigger the request, assert the loading UI immediately, then await the eventual success or failure UI.

keyPoints: Use Mock Service Worker to declaratively control API communication in tests.
Handlers describe server behavior while the component retains its ordinary request implementation.
In a Node-based test suite, create the mock server with MSW's `setupServer` function.
The server intercepts the API request issued by the component under test.
gotchas: Do not stub `window.fetch` for this scenario; use MSW's declarative request handlers rather than a fetch-specific adapter.

Async behavior::waitForElementToBeRemove.summary: Wait for an existing DOM element or collection to be removed, typically after an asynchronous user action or state change. It resolves when the target is gone and fails if no target exists at the start.
Async behavior::waitForElementToBeRemove.explanation: The helper waits until an element or collection is no longer in the DOM. It accepts the existing node directly or a callback that re-queries the DOM, and resolves after DOM mutations show removal; its options are passed through to waitFor.
Async behavior::waitForElementToBeRemove.syntax: function waitForElementToBeRemoved<T>(callback: (() => T) | T, options?: { container?: HTMLElement; timeout?: number; interval?: number; onTimeout?: (error: Error) => Error; mutationObserverOptions?: MutationObserverInit }): Promise<void>

parameters.name: callback
parameters.description: An element, an array of elements, or a callback returning an element or array of elements to remove.

parameters.name: options
parameters.type: { container?: HTMLElement; timeout?: number; interval?: number; onTimeout?: (error: Error) => Error; mutationObserverOptions?: MutationObserverInit }
parameters.description: Optional settings forwarded to waitFor, including container, timeout, interval, onTimeout, and mutationObserverOptions.

example.title: Wait for loading UI to disappear
example.explanation: Pass the initially rendered loading element, then await its removal before asserting the completed UI.

useCases.title: Await loading completion
useCases.scenario: A component displays a loading indicator while a request is pending.

useCases.title: Verify dismissal
useCases.scenario: A dismiss action removes a temporary alert or dialog.

useCases.title: Observe asynchronous disappearance
useCases.scenario: A user action causes a transient DOM node to be removed.

interview.question: What does waitForElementToBeRemoved do?
interview.answer: It waits for an element or collection to be removed from the DOM and returns a Promise. The argument may be the element(s) themselves or a callback that returns them.
interview.followUp: Why can a callback be useful? It can re-query after DOM mutations, so it observes the current matching node rather than relying only on a previously captured reference.

interview.question: What happens if the initial target is absent?
interview.answer: The target must already exist when waiting begins. A null value or empty array is rejected because there is nothing to wait to disappear.
interview.followUp: What assertion pattern is appropriate when the element may not exist initially? Use waitFor with a query that returns null and assert that the result is absent, rather than calling this helper.

interview.question: How does it detect removal and relate to waitFor?
interview.answer: The helper is a wrapper around waitFor and uses DOM mutation observation to detect removal. It resolves when the observed element or elements are gone.
interview.followUp: How does this differ from manually polling? MutationObserver reacts to relevant DOM changes instead of repeatedly checking at fixed intervals.

keyPoints: Use this helper when a user-visible node should disappear after an asynchronous action completes.
Provide one node, multiple nodes, or a function returning either form.
A callback should return the element or elements whose disappearance is being awaited.
The documentation describes resolution after removal; the current API signature returns a Promise<void>.
Removal detection uses MutationObserver, making it more efficient than regular polling with waitFor.
gotchas: The element must exist when waiting starts; passing null or an empty array fails immediately.
Do not use a query result that already indicates absence as the initial target.
Timeout and observer-related behavior can be configured through the waitFor options.

Interactions::Testing forms.summary: Test forms by finding controls through accessible labels or roles, performing real user interactions, and asserting the submitted values or resulting UI state. Await asynchronous interactions and outcomes.
Interactions::Testing forms.explanation: Render the form, locate controls as a user would, enter values with userEvent, submit it, and assert the callback payload. For asynchronous submission, wait until the expected outcome occurs.
Interactions::Testing forms.syntax:
const user = userEvent.setup()
await user.type(screen.getByRole('textbox', {name: /field label/i}), value)
await user.click(screen.getByRole('button', {name: /submit/i}))
await waitFor(() => expect(onSubmit).toHaveBeenCalledWith(values))

example.title: Test a form submission
example.explanation: The test finds fields and the submit control by accessible roles and names, performs realistic user actions, then waits for the submitted values.

useCases.title: Successful submission
useCases.scenario: A user fills required fields and submits a form; assert that the submission handler receives the entered values.

useCases.title: Asynchronous validation
useCases.scenario: A form performs delayed validation or submission; wait for the resulting error or success state before asserting it.

useCases.title: Accessible interaction flow
useCases.scenario: A component exposes fields through labels and roles; verify the complete flow without relying on component instances or internal state.

interview.question: How do you test a form submission from the user’s perspective?
interview.answer: Use render to mount the form, userEvent.setup to create a user interaction instance, then locate fields and the submit button with accessible queries. Type values, click Submit, and assert the callback received the expected object, waiting when the result is asynchronous.
interview.followUp: How would you test delayed validation? Await the interaction, then use waitFor or a find* query to observe the error or successful state instead of ending the test immediately.

interview.question: Which queries should a form test prefer?
interview.answer: Use queries based on the control’s accessible role and name, such as getByRole('textbox', {name: /email/i}). This avoids coupling the test to component instances or internal implementation details.
interview.followUp: What selector is an escape hatch when meaningful text or labels are impractical? A data-testid can be used, but accessible queries should remain the default.

interview.question: Why use userEvent and asynchronous assertions together?
interview.answer: Create the interaction instance with userEvent.setup(), perform each action with await, and then assert the visible or submitted result. This models user behavior more closely than directly invoking event handlers.
interview.followUp: Why wait for the result rather than only checking that a click occurred? The application may update asynchronously after the interaction, so waiting verifies the user-observable outcome.

keyPoints: Choose queries that resemble user discovery, especially accessible roles and names for form controls.
Associate labels with fields and query the resulting controls by their accessible names.
Use userEvent to enter values through the rendered controls rather than calling component handlers directly.
Submit through the actual button interaction, then verify the resulting callback or UI state.
Assert the complete submitted value object, including each field value the user entered.
gotchas: Prefer accessible roles and names over implementation-specific selectors so the test reflects how users find controls.

Interactions::userEvent interactions.summary: React Testing Library's user-event models realistic browser interactions such as typing, clicking, keyboard input, and tabbing. Prefer it over direct event dispatch when testing how users operate the UI.
Interactions::userEvent interactions.explanation: `user-event` models interactions at the user level: create a configured session, then await methods such as typing, clicking, keyboard input, or tabbing. It performs browser-oriented checks and may dispatch several events, making tests closer to real use than directly firing one DOM event.
Interactions::userEvent interactions.syntax:
const user = userEvent.setup()
await user.click(element)
await user.type(element, text)
await user.keyboard(text)
await user.tab()

example.title: Typing with userEvent
example.explanation: Create a user-event session, render the component, then await interaction methods so the test follows browser-like input behavior.

useCases.title: Model text entry
useCases.scenario: A form test needs to enter text and verify validation or submission behavior.

useCases.title: Exercise pointer interactions
useCases.scenario: A component changes state after a button, checkbox, or link is activated.

useCases.title: Test keyboard and focus behavior
useCases.scenario: A workflow depends on focus movement, held keys, shortcuts, or keyboard navigation.

useCases.title: Compose multi-step interactions
useCases.scenario: A test needs to reproduce a sequence of actions while preserving pressed-key state.

interview.question: How does user-event differ from fireEvent?
interview.answer: user-event describes a user interaction and simulates the resulting browser behavior, while fireEvent dispatches a DOM event directly. A single user action can therefore produce multiple events and additional checks.
interview.followUp: When would fireEvent still be appropriate? Use it when the required interaction or aspect is not implemented by user-event and the code relies on a specific concrete event.

interview.question: How should a test initialize user-event?
interview.answer: Call `userEvent.setup()` to create an interaction session, then invoke methods on the returned object. The session keeps input-device state across consecutive interactions, so sequences such as holding a key and clicking can behave consistently.
interview.followUp: Why set up before render? The documentation recommends creating the session before rendering so its workarounds are applied before the component is mounted.

interview.question: Why prefer user-event for interaction tests?
interview.answer: Use the session methods to express actions such as typing, clicking, keyboard input, and tabbing rather than dispatching implementation-level events. Await those interaction calls because the APIs return promises.
interview.followUp: What does setup configure besides methods? It applies user-event workarounds to the document and can configure an instance, including clipboard support for workflows that need it.

keyPoints: It models the browser event sequence produced by a user action rather than sending only one chosen event.
Choose user-event when the test should represent an interaction; reserve fireEvent for direct event dispatch.
Interactions include checks that help reject actions a real user could not perform.
The library updates the DOM through browser-like interaction behavior, improving confidence in UI tests.
A setup instance preserves device state across calls, which supports realistic multi-step keyboard and pointer sequences.
Related calls can be composed into one realistic user workflow.
gotchas: Initialize the user session before rendering the component.
Not every browser interaction is implemented; use fireEvent only for a concrete event that user-event cannot describe.
Clipboard workflows need the setup-provided clipboard stub when the test environment is not secure.

Interactions::userEvent keyboard flows.summary: Simulate realistic keyboard input with `userEvent.keyboard()`, including text, named keys, key codes, held modifiers, repetitions, and releases. Use it to test shortcuts and keyboard-driven behavior.
Interactions::userEvent keyboard flows.explanation: Use the instance returned by `userEvent.setup()` and await its keyboard methods. `keyboard` interprets printable characters and key descriptors, dispatches the corresponding interaction, and preserves pressed-key state so combinations and later actions behave consistently.

parameters.name: input
parameters.description: Keyboard actions expressed as printable characters or key descriptors using `{key}` and `[code]` notation.

example.title: Typing and activating a keyboard shortcut
example.explanation: Creates a user-event session, focuses the textbox, types text, and presses Enter as a single keyboard flow.

useCases.title: Text entry and activation
useCases.scenario: A user enters text and activates an action with Enter or another named key.

useCases.title: Keyboard shortcuts
useCases.scenario: A component responds to Ctrl, Shift, Alt, or Meta combinations.

useCases.title: Codes and localized layouts
useCases.scenario: A test must verify exact key codes or a non-US keyboard layout.

useCases.title: Held-key sequences
useCases.scenario: A flow needs to preserve modifier state across separate user interactions.

interview.question: What does `user.keyboard()` accept and how are keys represented?
interview.answer: `keyboard()` accepts a keyboard-input string and returns a promise. Printable characters are typed directly, while brace descriptors use `KeyboardEvent.key` names and bracket descriptors use `KeyboardEvent.code` names.
interview.followUp: How would you model a shortcut spanning multiple actions? Keep the modifier pressed with a `>` descriptor, perform the other action, then release it with a slash-prefixed descriptor.

interview.question: How should keyboard interactions be initialized in a test?
interview.answer: Call `userEvent.setup()` to create an instance, then await `user.keyboard(...)`. The instance tracks input-device state, including keys that remain pressed, across consecutive interactions.
interview.followUp: Why is setup preferable to isolated direct calls? A shared instance lets consecutive interactions preserve realistic device state and configuration.

interview.question: How can a test verify tab order and reverse tabbing?
interview.answer: Use `user.tab()` to move focus in browser-like order, and pass `{shift: true}` for reverse traversal. For a focus trap, provide its container through the tab API's focus-trap option.
interview.followUp: What limitation should be considered in jsdom? Native tabbing is absent, so focus-trap behavior may require the provided containment option or another test environment.

keyPoints: `keyboard()` models a sequence of keyboard actions rather than one isolated DOM event.
Pass one keyboard-input string to describe the intended sequence.
Plain printable text expands into individual character keystrokes.
Brace notation identifies keys by their `KeyboardEvent.key` values.
Bracket notation identifies keys by their `KeyboardEvent.code` values.
Keeping a modifier pressed lets the sequence represent shortcuts such as modifier-plus-key combinations.
gotchas: The default mapping models a US keyboard; pass a custom `keyboardMap` when the tested layout differs.
A key descriptor ending in `>` remains pressed until explicitly released or closed with `/`.

Queries::getByLabelText.summary: Find a form control through the text of its associated label, mirroring how users identify fields. Use it to expose missing or broken label associations in UI tests.
Queries::getByLabelText.explanation: `getByLabelText` first matches label text, then returns the form control associated with that label. With React Testing Library, use the `screen` version after rendering; it throws when no matching element is found, making broken label associations visible in the test.
Queries::getByLabelText.syntax: getByLabelText(container: HTMLElement, text: TextMatch, options?: { selector?: string; exact?: boolean; normalizer?: NormalizerFn }): HTMLElement

parameters.name: text
parameters.description: The label text to match; a string, regular expression, or function.

parameters.name: options
parameters.type: { selector?: string; exact?: boolean; normalizer?: NormalizerFn }
parameters.description: Optional matching controls: `selector`, `exact`, and `normalizer`.

parameters.name: container
parameters.description: The root element for the DOM Testing Library form; omit it when using `screen`.

Queries::getByLabelText.returns: The matching associated element as an HTMLElement; the `getBy` variant throws when no match is found.

example.title: Find a labeled form control
example.explanation: The query locates the input associated with the visible label text.

useCases.title: Locate labeled form controls
useCases.scenario: A form field has a visible `<label>` associated with an input, textarea, or other control.

useCases.title: Catch accessibility regressions
useCases.scenario: A label-to-control association is accidentally removed during a UI change.

useCases.title: Narrow matching with a selector
useCases.scenario: A test must distinguish a particular control among elements associated with similar label text.

interview.question: What does `getByLabelText` do?
interview.answer: It matches the supplied text against a label and then returns the element associated with that label. This models how users identify form controls through visible label text.
interview.followUp: How can the query be restricted to a particular control type? Pass an options object such as `{selector: 'input'}`.

interview.question: Why can React tests call `screen.getByLabelText` without a container?
interview.answer: The `screen` form omits the container because React Testing Library binds queries to the rendered base element. The DOM Testing Library form receives the container first.
interview.followUp: What is the DOM form's signature? `getByLabelText(container, text, options?)`.

interview.question: What kinds of matcher and options does it accept?
interview.answer: Its primary text argument accepts a string, regular expression, or function through the `TextMatch` type. Options include `selector`, `exact`, and `normalizer`.
interview.followUp: When might `getByRole` be preferable? A role query with an accessible name is more robust if the implementation changes to `aria-label` or `aria-labelledby`.

keyPoints: The query performs two steps: match label text, then resolve that label to its associated control.
In React tests, call `screen.getByLabelText(text, options?)`; the container is already bound.
The options support a selector and exact matching, with exact matching enabled by default.
A custom normalizer can control how candidate label text is normalized before matching.
Text matching is not reliable when the label content is fragmented across elements.
gotchas: A label whose text is split across nested elements may not match as expected; use a role query with an accessible name when appropriate.
When several associated controls could match, constrain the result with the `selector` option.

Queries::getByText and getByTestId.summary: Use `getByText` for user-visible text and reserve `getByTestId` for cases where role or text cannot express the intended match. Each is a single-element query and throws if it finds zero or multiple matches.
Queries::getByText and getByTestId.explanation: `getByText` searches an element's text content, while `getByTestId` searches the `data-testid` attribute. Both are single-element queries: they return one match and throw when there is no match or when multiple elements match.

parameters.name: textOrTestId
parameters.description: Text or test ID to match; the primary matcher may be a string, regular expression, or function.

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: Optional query options, including options affecting text parsing.

Queries::getByText and getByTestId.returns: The single matching element; throws a descriptive error if no element matches or if more than one element matches.

example.title: Choosing between text and test ID
example.explanation: Use the visible text query when that is how users identify the content; use the test ID only for an element that lacks a suitable user-facing query.

useCases.title: Locate visible content
useCases.scenario: A paragraph, heading, label-like message, or other non-interactive content is identified by what it displays.

useCases.title: Use a stable test ID
useCases.scenario: Text changes dynamically or no suitable role or visible text can express the intended target.

useCases.title: Assert a unique element
useCases.scenario: A rendered component is checked for exactly one expected match.

interview.question: What is the difference between getByText and getByTestId?
interview.answer: `getByText` locates elements through their text content and is useful for non-interactive elements such as divs, spans, and paragraphs. `getByTestId` locates an element through its `data-testid` attribute.
interview.followUp: Why should test IDs not be the default? They are not visible or audible to users, so role or text is usually a more user-centered locator.

interview.question: What happens when a getBy query finds zero or multiple elements?
interview.answer: A singular `getBy...` query returns the matching node when exactly one match exists. It throws a descriptive error if no element matches or if multiple elements match.
interview.followUp: What should be used for multiple expected matches? Use `getAllBy...`; for asynchronous appearance, use `findBy...`.

interview.question: When is getByTestId appropriate?
interview.answer: Use `getByText` when the user-facing text is the meaningful way to identify the element. Reserve `getByTestId` for cases where role or text cannot identify it, such as dynamic text or a missing semantic match.
interview.followUp: How can an asynchronous element be queried? Use the corresponding `findBy...` query, which returns a promise and retries until the default timeout.

keyPoints: Testing Library queries locate rendered elements in the page under test.
`getByText` is suitable for non-interactive elements, including ordinary containers and text blocks.
`getByTestId` targets implementation-facing metadata rather than something users perceive.
Choose a test ID when role or text is unavailable or does not make sense.
The query matcher can be a string, regular expression, or function.
gotchas: A test ID is invisible to users, so prefer a role or text query when one is appropriate.
For non-form content, text is generally the user-facing way to locate the element.
Do not use a singular getBy query when zero or multiple matches are expected; use an appropriate query variant instead.

Queries::within.summary: Use `within` to bind Testing Library queries to a DOM element. This scopes later searches to that element, which is useful for controls inside cards, dialogs, or repeated regions.
Queries::within.explanation: `within` turns a DOM element into a set of queries bound to that element. In React Testing Library, use it after locating a card, dialog, or repeated region so subsequent queries cannot match similar controls elsewhere in the rendered document.

parameters.name: element
parameters.description: The DOM element whose descendants should be searched by the returned query functions.

Queries::within.returns: An object containing query functions bound to the supplied DOM element.

example.title: Scope a query to one region
example.explanation: Create a scoped query object from a DOM element, then use its bound queries to search only that element's descendants.

useCases.title: Repeated components
useCases.scenario: A page contains multiple cards with identically named buttons; locate one card first and query its button.

useCases.title: Dialogs
useCases.scenario: A dialog has controls whose names also appear behind the overlay; scope queries to the dialog element.

useCases.title: Nested regions
useCases.scenario: A message panel contains repeated text or actions that should not match content elsewhere.

interview.question: What does `within` do?
interview.answer: `within` accepts a DOM element and returns query functions bound to that element. This lets a test search only inside the chosen region instead of the whole document.
interview.followUp: How is this related to `getQueriesForElement`? `within` is an alias for that function.

interview.question: How would you test a control inside a specific card?
interview.answer: First locate the container with a query such as `getByRole`, then call `within(container)` and use the returned methods, such as `getByRole` or `getByText`. The bound methods do not need the container passed again.
interview.followUp: Why prefer this over global queries? It makes repeated regions unambiguous and prevents a match in an unrelated region.

interview.question: How does `within` relate to React Testing Library's `render` and `screen` queries?
interview.answer: React Testing Library uses `within` under the hood for queries returned by `render`. Those queries are already bound to the rendered base element, while an explicit `within` scopes them to a narrower DOM node.
interview.followUp: What is the common alternative for document-wide queries? Use `screen`, whose queries are pre-bound to `document.body`.

keyPoints: The public `within` name is an alias of `getQueriesForElement`.
It produces query methods whose search container is the supplied element.
React Testing Library uses this scoping mechanism internally for its rendered queries.
A typical call chains `within` with a query method to find content inside a selected region.
gotchas: Pass the actual DOM element, not a text label or arbitrary selector, to `within`.
After scoping, call the returned query methods without supplying a container argument.

Test design::Accessibility assertions.summary: Test accessible UI contracts by querying semantic roles and accessible names, checking relevant states, and exercising keyboard behavior with realistic user interactions.
Test design::Accessibility assertions.explanation: Design component tests around the interface exposed to users: locate controls by semantic role and accessible name, assert relevant ARIA states, and simulate keyboard interactions rather than inspecting implementation details.

parameters.name: container
parameters.description: The DOM container in which to search.

parameters.name: role
parameters.description: The semantic or ARIA role to match.

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: Optional filters including accessible name, description, states, visibility, level, and value.

Test design::Accessibility assertions.returns: The matching element or elements, depending on the query variant.

example.title: Accessible button test
example.explanation: Find the control by its semantic role and accessible name, inspect its state, then exercise keyboard interaction through user-event.

useCases.title: Accessible form controls
useCases.scenario: A form control must remain discoverable by its label or accessible name.

useCases.title: Stateful widgets
useCases.scenario: A toggle, checkbox, tab, or disclosure exposes a state that users can observe.

useCases.title: Keyboard interaction
useCases.scenario: A component must respond correctly to Tab, Enter, Space, or other keyboard input.

interview.question: How do you find a button by its accessible identity?
interview.answer: getByRole queries elements using their semantic role, including implicit roles such as button. Its name option filters by accessible name, which commonly comes from a label, button text, or aria-label.
interview.followUp: Why prefer this over getByText for a button? Because it checks the semantic role and accessible name together, reflecting how users and assistive technologies identify the control.

interview.question: How do you assert accessibility-related state?
interview.answer: Pass state filters to getByRole when the role supports them. The documentation lists options such as selected, busy, checked, pressed, current, and expanded.
interview.followUp: How can hidden content be included? Set hidden: true, which considers elements normally excluded from the accessibility tree.

interview.question: How should keyboard behavior be tested?
interview.answer: Use user-event for interaction tests because it simulates browser-like interactions and performs visibility and interactability checks. For keyboard coverage, use its keyboard API with a key-action descriptor.
interview.followUp: Why not rely only on fireEvent? fireEvent dispatches DOM events, while user-event models the fuller interaction that can produce multiple events and checks.

keyPoints: Use getByRole to locate controls through semantic roles, optionally matching the accessible name.
Implicit roles count, so native elements usually need no explicit role attribute in the test.
Accessible name or description narrows results when several elements share a role.
Role queries can target checked state with checked: true or checked: false.
gotchas: Prefer getByRole with the expected role and name over a text-only query when testing an interactive element.
Using hidden: true includes elements normally excluded from the accessibility tree, so apply it only when the test intentionally targets them.
Fallback roles require queryFallbacks: true; otherwise the query uses the primary role.

Test design::Avoiding implementation det.summary: Write tests around what users can find and do in the rendered UI, not component state, private methods, lifecycle methods, or child-component structure. This makes tests more resilient to implementation-only refactors.
Test design::Avoiding implementation det.explanation: Render the component, locate controls through the same accessible signals users rely on, perform a realistic interaction, and assert the resulting DOM. Avoid component instances, state, lifecycle methods, private methods, and child-component internals so implementation refactors do not invalidate behavior-focused tests.

example.title: Test behavior through the rendered UI
example.explanation: The test interacts with the rendered button and verifies visible output, without reading component state or calling private methods.

useCases.title: Refactor-resistant regression tests
useCases.scenario: A component’s internal state management changes while its visible behavior remains the same.

useCases.title: Accessible form workflows
useCases.scenario: A form must be tested from field discovery through submission feedback.

useCases.title: Stable parent behavior tests
useCases.scenario: A component contains implementation-only child components that may be reorganized.

interview.question: What does avoiding implementation details mean in React Testing Library?
interview.answer: Test the rendered DOM as a user would: find controls by accessible roles, names, labels, or visible text, interact with them, and assert observable output. This avoids coupling the test to component instances and private implementation.
interview.followUp: How should a test handle an element without meaningful text or labeling? Use the documented data-testid escape hatch only when text or a label is not sensible or practical.

interview.question: What should a test assert instead of component state?
interview.answer: A behavior test verifies what users can see and do, such as submitting a form and observing a confirmation. It should not inspect component state, invoke internal methods, or assert lifecycle calls.
interview.followUp: Why is this valuable during refactoring? Changes to implementation without functional changes are less likely to break the test.

interview.question: How do accessible queries support user-centered tests?
interview.answer: Use DOM nodes and queries that resemble how users find elements, rather than component instances or arbitrary selectors. For interactions, user-event models browser interactions more completely than dispatching isolated DOM events.
interview.followUp: When might fireEvent still be appropriate? Use it for interactions or event aspects that user-event does not yet implement, accepting the added reliance on concrete event details.

keyPoints: Model tests on real user workflows; similarity to actual use is the library’s confidence-building principle.
Keeping tests independent of internals helps implementation-only refactors avoid unnecessary failures.
Treat state as an implementation detail rather than a direct assertion target.
Do not call private component methods to arrange or verify behavior.
Lifecycle execution is not the user-facing contract and should not drive ordinary tests.
gotchas: Do not treat internal state, internal methods, lifecycle methods, or child components as the primary test contract.

Test design::Cleanup and isolation.summary: Reset test state by unmounting every React tree rendered during a test. Cleanup is automatic with supported global afterEach hooks; otherwise, register cleanup explicitly after each test.
Test design::Cleanup and isolation.explanation: React Testing Library’s cleanup unmounts React trees created by render. Test runners that provide a global afterEach hook register it automatically; otherwise, call cleanup from the framework’s per-test hook to prevent leftover DOM and non-isolated tests.
Test design::Cleanup and isolation.returns: The page documents cleanup as a teardown function that unmounts React trees mounted by render; it does not specify a return value.

example.title: Explicit cleanup with AVA
example.explanation: Register cleanup with the test runner’s per-test hook so each rendered React tree is unmounted after the test.

useCases.title: Use automatic teardown
useCases.scenario: A Jest, Mocha, or Jasmine suite exposes a global afterEach hook.

useCases.title: Register cleanup manually
useCases.scenario: An AVA suite needs explicit per-test teardown.

useCases.title: Prevent cross-test contamination
useCases.scenario: A test suite must avoid leaked renders affecting later tests.

interview.question: What does cleanup do, and when is it automatic?
interview.answer: cleanup unmounts the React trees mounted by render. When the test framework supplies a global afterEach hook, React Testing Library invokes cleanup automatically; otherwise, register cleanup yourself after each test.
interview.followUp: What should an AVA test suite do? Register test.afterEach(cleanup), because AVA does not provide the global hook that triggers automatic registration.

interview.question: How do you enforce isolation in a framework without automatic cleanup?
interview.answer: Call cleanup after every test that uses render, typically through the framework’s per-test hook. This removes the mounted React trees and keeps later tests independent.
interview.followUp: What failure modes can omission cause? It can produce memory leaks and non-idempotent tests that are difficult to debug.

interview.question: How would you configure cleanup in AVA?
interview.answer: Import cleanup from @testing-library/react and pass it to the test runner’s after-each mechanism, as in test.afterEach(cleanup). This ensures teardown happens after each test.
interview.followUp: Why not clean up only once per suite? A single teardown does not isolate tests that run before it; per-test cleanup is required.

keyPoints: cleanup removes React trees created by render.
Automatic cleanup is available when the framework injects a global afterEach hook.
Frameworks without that hook require explicit cleanup after every test.
In AVA, register cleanup directly with test.afterEach.
gotchas: Omitting cleanup after render can leak memory.
Without cleanup, tests may depend on execution order or fail because earlier renders remain.
